questions.q: You disagree with a proposal but want to remain respectful. What do you say?
o: I see your point, although I have a different view.
That is completely foolish.
You are wrong, end of story.
I refuse to hear your idea.
questions.e: This acknowledges the other view before disagreeing.

questions.q: You want to qualify a claim because the evidence is limited. What do you say?
o: This is certainly true in every case.
The evidence suggests this may be the case.
Nobody can ever know anything.
The evidence was a suggestion.
questions.e: “Suggests” presents a cautious conclusion.

questions.q: A colleague proposes a useful revision. How do you respond?
o: That suggestion is constructed.
I suggest you are useful.
That is a constructive suggestion.
It is useful yesterday.
questions.e: “Constructive suggestion” means helpful proposal.

questions.q: You want to return to the main topic of a discussion. What do you say?
o: Let us return the discussion point.
We returned from the topic.
The point has returned us.
Let us return to the point under discussion.
questions.e: This phrase brings a discussion back on topic.

questions.q: You need to interrupt politely during a presentation. What do you say?
o: May I add something here?
I will stop your presentation.
You add something yesterday.
May I interrupt you forever?
questions.e: This is a courteous way to contribute.

questions.q: You want to emphasize that a plan is still uncertain. What do you say?
o: The plan is still a subject change.
The plan is still subject to change.
The subject is planning still.
The plan changed the subject.
questions.e: “Subject to change” means it may change later.

questions.q: You are presenting a conclusion that follows from earlier evidence. What do you say?
o: Taken separately, these findings forget that…
These findings take us together.
Taken together, these findings indicate that…
The conclusion is taking evidence.
questions.e: This signals a conclusion based on combined findings.

questions.q: You want to propose a compromise. What do you say?
o: Could we meet at the halfway?
We met half yesterday.
This is halfway to meet.
Could we meet halfway on this?
questions.e: “Meet halfway” means each side makes a concession.

questions.q: A speaker made a valid point you had not considered. What do you say?
o: That is a fair point; I had not considered it.
That is a point of fairness yesterday.
I considered your point unfairly.
Your point is not considered.
questions.e: This acknowledges a reasonable argument.

questions.q: You want to politely ask for clarification of a term. What do you say?
o: Can you clear what equity means?
Could you clarify what you mean by “equity”?
Could you clarify equity yesterday?
What does you mean by clear?
questions.e: “Clarify” asks someone to make an idea clearer.

questions.q: You want to postpone a decision until more information is available. What do you say?
o: We should reserve the information from judgment.
We judged the reservation yesterday.
We should reserve judgment until we have more information.
We should decide without the facts.
questions.e: “Reserve judgment” means wait before deciding.

questions.q: You want to describe a result that was unexpected but understandable. What do you say?
o: In prospect, the outcome makes past.
The outcome retrospects us.
It makes sense before it happened.
In retrospect, the outcome makes sense.
questions.e: “In retrospect” looks back with later understanding.

questions.q: You want to show that a concern is important but not the only one. What do you say?
o: That is a valid concern, but it is not the whole picture.
That concern is the whole picture validly.
There is no concern in the picture.
The picture is concerned.
questions.e: This recognizes the concern while adding perspective.

questions.q: You want to state a limitation in your research. What do you say?
o: One limit is this studying small.
One limitation of this study is its small sample.
The study is limited small sample yesterday.
The sample studies its limitation.
questions.e: This clearly introduces a research limitation.

questions.q: You want to draw attention to an important difference. What do you say?
o: It is important to distinct the cases between.
The cases are importantly differented.
It is important to distinguish between the two cases.
We distinguish importance from cases.
questions.e: “Distinguish between” means identify how things differ.

questions.q: You want to make a recommendation based on evidence. What do you say?
o: At the basis of these results, we recommend…
By the base results, we are recommend…
These results are the recommendation basis to.
On the basis of these results, we recommend…
questions.e: “On the basis of” introduces supporting evidence.

questions.q: You want to correct a misunderstanding without blaming anyone. What do you say?
o: Perhaps I was unclear; what I meant was…
You misunderstood me, obviously.
You are unclear what I meant.
Perhaps the meaning was me.
questions.e: This gently takes responsibility and explains again.

questions.q: You want to say two developments happened together. What do you say?
o: These changes walk in one hand.
These changes go hand in hand.
These changes give hands.
We hand the changes together yesterday.
questions.e: “Go hand in hand” means happen together or are connected.

questions.q: You want to make your claim less absolute. What do you say?
o: This depends surely on every context.
The context likely depends it.
This is likely to depend on the context.
It is unlikely to contextualize.
questions.e: “Likely to” expresses probability, not certainty.

questions.q: You want to introduce a counterargument. What do you say?
o: Some may say the policy argued them.
The policy may argue the cost.
Some argue to costly.
Some may argue that the policy is too costly.
questions.e: “Some may argue” introduces another viewpoint.

questions.q: You want to explain that a measure had an unintended effect. What do you say?
o: The measure had the unintended consequence of delaying access.
The measure intended the consequence access.
The access measured the intention.
The consequence was measuring access.
questions.e: “Unintended consequence” describes an effect not planned.

questions.q: You want to stress that the issue needs further study. What do you say?
o: Further research was needed after the conclusion.
Further research is needed before we reach a conclusion.
We concluded before further research is needed.
The conclusion researches further.
questions.e: This states that evidence is not yet sufficient.

questions.q: You want to acknowledge a mistake in a formal discussion. What do you say?
o: I am standing correct yesterday.
You are corrected by me.
I stand corrected; thank you for pointing that out.
I point out your thank you.
questions.e: “I stand corrected” accepts that your earlier statement was wrong.

questions.q: You want to end your presentation and invite questions. What do you say?
o: That concludes your question presentation.
My questions conclude you.
I welcome my presentation yesterday.
That concludes my presentation. I welcome your questions.
questions.e: This is a clear and polite closing.
